« Je ne veux pas d’étiquette » : pourquoi certains maires rechignent à parrainer les candidats de 2027
Pendant trois jours, le Parc des expositions de la porte de Versailles devient un passage obligé pour les prétendants à l’Élysée. À l’occasion du 108e Congrès de l’Association des maires de France (AMF), les élus locaux sont au cœur des convoitises. Dans les allées, Édouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, Raphaël Glucksmann, Dominique de Villepin, Fabien Roussel, Éric Zemmour, Teddy Riner, Nicolas Dupont-Aignan et Marine Tondelier multiplient les échanges. Tous ont en ligne de mire les 500 parrainages nécessaires pour concourir en 2027. Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Mélenchon, eux, manquent à l’appel.
Car derrière les poignées de main se joue déjà une bataille décisive, celle des signatures. Instauré en 1962, le dispositif impose à chaque candidat de réunir 500 parrainages d’élus, issus d’au moins 30 départements ou territoires, sans qu’un même territoire puisse en fournir plus de 10 %. Si députés, sénateurs et conseillers locaux peuvent apporter leur soutien, les maires en sont les principaux pourvoyeurs, ils représentaient près de 70 % des signatures validées en 2022.
Encore faut-il qu’ils acceptent de s’engager. Sur les quelque 42 000 élus habilités à parrainer, dont près de 35 000 maires, beaucoup hésitent à prendre position. Selon une enquête du Cevipof réalisée pour l’AMF et publiée le 20 novembre, 48,4 % des maires ne souhaitent accorder leur signature à aucun candidat. En 2022, plus de 40 candidats s’étaient lancés, mais seuls douze avaient franchi le cap des 500 parrainages.
La date limite, fixée au 12 mars, approche. Les formulaires officiels ne seront toutefois transmis aux équipes de campagne qu’en janvier ou février. D’ici là, les candidats devront transformer les poignées de main en promesses, puis les promesses en signatures. Et si les candidats ont déjà commencé à battre le pavé auprès des élus, les maires, eux, savent qu’ils seront particulièrement courtisés.
« Je ne veux pas que ma position politique soit affichée dans ma mairie »
Derrière les statistiques, les réticences des maires racontent une réalité bien plus concrète, celle d’élus locaux qui ne veulent pas voir leur fonction transformée en instrument de positionnement politique national. Dans une commune de l’Yonne qu’il dirige depuis dix-huit ans, un maire, qui préfère témoigner anonymement, résume cette inquiétude : « J’ai ma position politique, mais je ne veux pas qu’elle soit affichée au sein de ma mairie. » Les sollicitations sont devenues presque quotidiennes. « On reçoit dans les boîtes mail des mairies trois demandes de parrainage par semaine. » Certains démarcheurs vont même jusqu’à se présenter directement au domicile des élus. « Il y a parfois des demandes fantaisistes. »
Pour les maires des petites communes, où les relations personnelles et les équilibres locaux sont particulièrement sensibles, la signature publique peut rapidement devenir embarrassante. C’est notamment le cas d’une maire sans étiquette du Puy-de-Dôme, à la tête d’un village de 80 habitants. Pour elle, la question ne se pose même pas, elle ne parrainera aucun candidat. « Ça créerait trop de grabuge de se positionner politiquement. » Dans ces territoires où tout le monde se connaît, une signature peut être interprétée comme une prise de position personnelle, voire comme « un soutien politique de toute la municipalité ».
Georges Matichard, maire de Bonnevaux, dans le Gard, partage cette crainte. Élu depuis mars, il a construit son équipe municipale sans étiquette, en prenant soin de dépasser les clivages partisans. Il ne souhaite pas remettre en cause cet équilibre à l’occasion de la présidentielle. « On nous demande de coller une étiquette parce que c’est rendu public. Pour moi, c’est inacceptable. » Dans sa commune, explique-t-il, « une signature pourrait immédiatement provoquer des tensions au sein de son conseil municipal comme dans la population ». « J’aurai beau raconter ce que je veux, voilà, je vais avoir une étiquette. Dès le départ, on avait bien refusé de faire comme ça. » Pour cet élu, le problème tient à une contradiction fondamentale : « Le droit de vote doit être complètement anonyme. C’est en ça qu’il est grand et qu’il est fort. » Rendre public le parrainage revient, à ses yeux, à exposer les élus à « une forme de pression politique » qu’ils n’ont pas souhaitée.
Même prudence chez Christine Nadau, maire de Changé, en Mayenne. Élue sur une liste sans étiquette, elle entend conserver cette ligne de conduite jusqu’au bout : « Je ne signerai aucune demande pour garder cette ligne. » Au-delà de cette neutralité revendiquée, elle peine également à identifier un candidat qui lui inspire suffisamment confiance. « Parmi tous les candidats, je n’en vois pas un qui se détache du lot et qui pourrait être le sauveur, entre guillemets, de la France d’aujourd’hui. »
« Il faut qu’on donne notre voix au candidat qui sera à même de représenter le territoire »
Tous les maires ne partagent pourtant pas cette volonté de rester à l’écart. Certains revendiquent au contraire le parrainage comme un acte démocratique qui dépasse les affinités partisanes. C’est le cas de Laurence Pagès-Touzé, maire de Sainte-Radegonde, en Aveyron. Lors des précédentes élections présidentielles, elle avait choisi de parrainer un petit candidat, différent de celui pour lequel elle avait voté : « J’ai fait le choix de parrainer un petit candidat qui n’était pas le candidat pour qui j’ai voté, mais plus dans une logique de faire la pluralité des candidats. »
Déjà sollicitée, elle estime néanmoins que le système actuel mérite d’être interrogé. « Cette règle des 500 parrainages de maires, je trouve qu’on est peut-être au bout de ce système. » Pour autant, elle ne souhaite pas précipiter sa décision. Elle attend de voir comment la campagne va évoluer et surtout que les candidats dépassent les simples déclarations d’intention. « Ce qu’on attend, c’est une vision, des projets. »
Même approche chez Damien Pendaries, maire d’Agen-d’Aveyron, une commune de 1 100 habitants. Pour son premier mandat, il découvre l’intensité de cette course aux signatures, qui dépasse largement les grandes villes et les territoires les plus politisés. « L’autre jour, j’ai vu deux émissaires du Parti communiste français envoyés de Paris au fin fond de l’Aveyron », raconte-t-il. S’il s’interroge sur la pertinence du seuil des 500 signatures et sur le nombre de candidats susceptibles de se présenter, il estime néanmoins que les maires ont une responsabilité à exercer. « Il faut qu’on donne notre voix au candidat qui sera à même de représenter le territoire. Parce que la signature, ce n’est pas une signature individuelle. On représente un territoire, on représente une commune. »
Une conception du parrainage qui se heurte toutefois à celle d’autres élus, davantage soucieux de préserver leur neutralité. À Ménilles, dans l’Eure, Didier Courtrat a même choisi de trancher collectivement. Dans cette commune de 1 800 habitants, le conseil municipal a décidé de ne parrainer aucun candidat. « Nous avons décidé collectivement de ne pas désigner un candidat favorisé par une signature. » L’élu ne souhaite pas transformer le fonctionnement de sa municipalité en débat partisan. Les sollicitations sont pourtant nombreuses, et certaines méthodes le dérangent : « Il y en a certains, je trouve qu’ils sont un petit peu agressif. On sent bien que si on ne leur donne pas la signature, ils nous le reprochent un petit peu quand même. »
Dans une commune proche de Toulon, un maire sans étiquette envisage, lui, une autre stratégie, celle d’attendre le dernier moment. « À la toute fin, on fera le choix de parrainer, mais seulement si certains qui, pour nous, représentent la démocratie n’en ont pas assez. »
Si les candidats ont besoin des maires pour entrer dans la compétition présidentielle, ces derniers n’entendent pas pour autant devenir les acteurs d’une campagne qui n’est pas la leur.
Le Congrès des maires, théâtre des ambitions présidentielles
Face à ces réticences, les prétendants à l’Élysée tentent de rassurer. Le congrès de l’AMF constitue une occasion privilégiée de rencontrer les élus, de présenter leurs propositions et de faire valoir leur conception du rôle des collectivités. David Lisnard, maire de Cannes et président de l’AMF, entend défendre le principe d’un parrainage libéré de toute pression politique. Il appelle les maires à ne pas confondre signature et adhésion à un programme. « Vous êtes de gauche, n’hésitez pas à donner votre parrainage à un type dont vous ne partagez pas les convictions, mais qui représente une frange de la population », plaide-t-il. Pour lui, le parrainage doit avant tout garantir la pluralité démocratique. Il défend depuis plusieurs années le retour à l’anonymat des signatures et affirme avoir interpellé successivement plusieurs Premiers ministres sur le sujet, sans obtenir de réponse. « Il est important de déstresser les maires là-dessus », insiste-t-il, appelant les élus à ne pas vivre cette échéance comme un engagement partisan.
Certains maires ont néanmoins déjà fait leur choix. C’est le cas de Martine Finiels, maire de Vernoux-en-Vivarais, en Ardèche, qui a décidé d’apporter son parrainage à Raphaël Glucksmann. Pour elle, ce geste s’inscrit dans une pratique démocratique qu’elle revendique depuis plusieurs mandats. « J’ai fait mon troisième mandat et j’ai toujours parrainé effectivement un candidat à la présidentielle. » La campagne des parrainages lui est d’ailleurs déjà très concrète : « J’ai même eu des militants de candidats qui sont venus frapper à ma porte, à mon domicile, pour demander un parrainage. » Une démarche qui témoigne de l’intensification du démarchage engagé par les équipes en quête de signatures.
Denis Durand, maire divers gauche de Vengy-sur-Craon, a lui aussi promis son parrainage à Natacha Polony, dont il partage les priorités, notamment sur l’éducation. « C’est elle qui peut rassembler », estime-t-il, voyant dans sa candidature une alternative au « macronisme finissant ». Abonné à Marianne, il affirme avoir lui-même encouragé la journaliste à se lancer dans la course présidentielle. Venue à la rencontre des élus, Natacha Polony revendique l’importance de ce dialogue avec les maires. « Je suis venue discuter avec les premiers élus de la République », explique-t-elle, présentant le parrainage comme un « droit fondamental » permettant de faire vivre la démocratie.
D’autres candidats prennent toutefois leurs distances avec l’idée d’une chasse aux signatures. Fabien Roussel assure ainsi ne pas être venu au congrès de l’AMF pour chercher des parrainages. Même discours chez Raphaël Glucksmann : « Je ne suis pas là pour faire la course aux parrainages. » Des déclarations qui n’effacent pas la réalité de la compétition, aucun prétendant ne peut se permettre d’ignorer les élus locaux.
Dans ce ballet présidentiel, deux présences illustrent particulièrement les différentes étapes de cette course. Teddy Riner, qui affirme avoir déjà franchi la centaine de parrainages, reconnaît « le stress » que représente cette collecte. François Hollande, à l’inverse, n’a pas officiellement annoncé sa candidature, mais son passage dans les allées du Congrès suffit à alimenter les conversations. « Enfin, il est là », commentent certains maires. Pourtant, ceux qui ont croisé l’ancien président assurent : « Il ne m’a rien demandé ».
À la porte de Versailles, les ambitions présidentielles se croisent donc avec les hésitations des élus. Le contraste est saisissant. Pendant que les prétendants à l’Élysée cherchent à obtenir leur parrainage, les élus locaux attendent souvent qu’on s’intéresse d’abord à leurs difficultés et à celles de leurs administrés. Une chose est certaine, avant même que les électeurs ne soient appelés aux urnes, la présidentielle de 2027 se joue déjà, en partie, dans les mairies. Et ceux qui détiennent les clés de cette première étape ne sont pas nécessairement les plus pressés de les remettre.

L'Agence du médicament met en garde contre les conseils de l'IA qui "peuvent être dangereux" pour la santé des patients
De plus en plus de personnes se tournent vers l'intelligence artificielle pour demander un avis médical, notamment sur la prise de médicament. Mais cela n'est pas sans risque pour la santé et des surdosages peuvent provoquer des lésions irréversibles.
Les conseils de l'intelligence artificielle sur la prise de médicaments "peuvent être dangereux" pour la santé des patients, alerte l'Agence nationale de sécurité du médicament (ANSM) jeudi 26 novembre. L'agence a recensé au moins huit cas de surdosage en deux ans, entre 2024 et 2026, liés aux conseils donnés par une IA chez des personnes allant de 17 à 89 ans, la moitié ayant entre 17 et 19 ans. Une personne a dû être hospitalisée.
Ce chiffre paraît peu élevé mais "il est probable qu'il y ait une sous-estimation de la déclaration de ces types de cas", explique sur franceinfo le directeur adjoint de l'ANSM, Alexandre de la Volpilière. "On a un risque de voir se multiplier ce genre de situation", prévient-il.
Des surdosages avec des lésions irréversibles
L'ANSM cite deux cas de surdosage en paracétamol, qui peut provoquer des lésions irréversibles au foie. Une femme enceinte a, elle, pris une quantité trop importante d'antimigraineux après avoir suivi les indications de son IA. L'agence évoque également des surdosages d’antiallergiques, d’antibiotiques, de sédatifs ou d’anxiolytiques.
Ces patients utilisent l'IA pour faire de l'automédication, mais ils peuvent aussi parfois suivre "un conseil sur un médicament qu'on a sur ordonnance. Le patient peut se dire 'Je vais mieux, j'arrête mon traitement' ou augmenter ses doses", ajoute Alexandre de la Volpilière.
"On n'augmente pas ses doses tout seul, ni en demandant à une IA. On demande à un professionnel de santé", rappelle le directeur adjoint de l'ANSM. "Les outils d’IA peuvent fournir des informations inexactes, contradictoires ou inadaptées à une situation individuelle et vous mettre en danger", conclut l'agence dans un communiqué.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has urged his country to focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons “across multiple domains for different missions”.
Kim said North Korea’s nuclear material production capacity was being systematically expanded on Thursday, according to state media KCNA.
Maintaining North Korea’s status as a nuclear-weapons state was “absolutely inviolable”, Kim said during an inspection of nuclear material production and weapons research facilities. KCNA did not identify the facilities or their locations.
The country’s status would not change because of what he called “denuclearisation rhetoric from forces that ignore objective reality and failed to recognise the changed situation”.
“Our nuclear capability is now a reality,” he said, calling recent achievements in nuclear weapons production a major success in carrying out the country’s nuclear policy.
Any attempt to deny North Korea’s nuclear status, which it enshrined in its constitution in 2023, would be regarded as “an open declaration of war”, he said.
Kim said diversified use of tactical nuclear weapons was an “important and urgent task raised from tactical nukes’ military value in modern warfare and from the inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state”.

Kim’s statements come during a growing border dispute with South Korea over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified territory between the two countries, on September 21.
Seoul demanded an apology from Pyongyang in October after a joint South Korea-United Nations investigation found that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago.
Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council in response, accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion, and fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan less than a week later.
South Korea estimates that North Korea possesses between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads.

BRUSSELS — The European Commission on Wednesday rejected Washington’s claim that Europe is fueling global industrial overcapacity, after the Trump administration proposed a 15% tariff on the 27-country bloc.
“We will study the findings. At the same time we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” Olof Gill, the Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson, said in a statement.

Federal Court Blocks New Trump Birthright Citizenship Executive Order
WASHINGTON — A federal district court today blocked President Trump’s new executive order targeting birthright citizenship.  
The ruling stems from a lawsuit, Nathan v. Trump, brought by the American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of New Hampshire, ACLU of Maine, ACLU of Massachusetts, ACLU of the District of Columbia, Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus, and Democracy Defenders Fund on behalf of people subjected to the new executive order. 
The groups already secured a major Supreme Court victory concerning birthright citizenship in Trump v. Barbara in June. That decision affirmed protections for babies who would have been denied citizenship under Trump’s first failed birthright citizenship executive order. 
In its ruling this summer, the Supreme Court confirmed that the Constitution’s Citizenship Clause puts “the question of citizenship ‘once and forever [to] rest.’” Despite that, the administration is again trying to restrict birthright citizenship. 
In today’s ruling, the district court explained that “Barbara’s ink had scarcely dried when the President issued [the] second executive order,” but emphasized that “the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws.” 
The following is reaction to today’s ruling:
“The president keeps trying to rewrite the Constitution by executive fiat. Today's ruling reinforces, yet again, that he cannot,” said Winnie Kao, senior counsel at Asian Law Caucus. “Instead of addressing the real problems Americans face, the Trump administration is wasting taxpayer dollars on yet another attempt to strip birthright citizenship from US-born babies, threatening to throw government agencies and families into chaos. Birthright citizenship has allowed generations of immigrants to build, contribute, and make this country what it is.  We will continue to defend it.” 
“Enough is enough,” said Cody Wofsy, Deputy Director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year.  Third time is not the charm, and the President needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land.” 
“This should put to rest all attempts to limit the citizenship protections owed to any child born in the United States,” said Brittany Carter, assistant counsel at the Legal Defense Fund. “This ruling affirms that the Administration’s continued efforts to circumvent the Constitution will not stand, and upholds the rule of law rather than the vengeful whims of the executive.” 
“Today’s ruling is a victory for families across the country,” said Tianna Mays, legal director at Democracy Defenders Fund. “The court correctly stopped this unlawful order before it could inflict irreversible harm on America’s youngest citizens. We will continue protecting these guaranteed rights from these lawless attacks.” 
“Birthright citizenship is the law of the land — period. Cruel attacks on this core constitutional right must not be allowed to stand, which the court reaffirmed once again today,” said SangYeob Kim, director of the ACLU of New Hampshire’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. 
"The courts have yet again reaffirmed that babies born in the United States are citizens," said ACLU of Maine Legal Director Carol Garvan. "The president may keep signing unlawful executive orders, but the Supreme Court was clear when it ruled that neither the president nor Congress can end birthright citizenship.” 
“This ruling affirms that birthright citizenship is here to stay — and there is nothing President Trump can do about that,” said Carol Rose, executive director at the ACLU of Massachusetts. “The Trump administration must follow the law, acknowledge the constitutional rights of our clients, and abandon this futile effort to rewrite the Fourteenth Amendment.” 
“The court yet again affirmed that the government cannot concoct new exceptions to the constitutional principle of birthright citizenship,” said Scott Michelman, legal director of the ACLU of the District of Columbia. “This ruling will hopefully put an end to President Trump's cruel crusade against the country's youngest citizens.”

Does Treating Addiction Rebuild Lives? Evidence from Buprenorphine

ABSTRACT
Does treating addiction improve economic circumstances as well as health? Using two decades of 
Veterans Health Administration records on over 140,000 patients with opioid use disorder and 
consumer credit data, we exploit staggered facility-level buprenorphine adoption and quasi-random 
emergency physician assignment. A five-percentage-point increase in the share of clinicians with 
buprenorphine prescribing experience doubles overdose survivors’ long-term medication use and 
reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 3.7 percentage points. Instrumenting receipt yields a 22 
percent credit score gain. At $300,000 per statistical life-year, estimated survival benefits alone 
exceed added medical costs within three years

1 Introduction
Does treating addiction rebuild lives? Medical innovation can generate substantial welfare
gains (Murphy and Topel, 2006; Cutler and McClellan, 2001), but whether effective treatments
also improve patients’ economic circumstances is a separate question. Addiction presents a
demanding case because illness and disadvantage are closely intertwined. First, medications
shown to be effective in controlled trials may deliver smaller benefits in routine care, where
adherence is imperfect and patients often have serious medical or psychiatric conditions that
can exclude them from trials. Second, even when treatment succeeds clinically, the poverty,
mental illness, and social isolation that accompany addiction may continue to hold down
employment and financial stability. Whether medication improves economic circumstances
despite these obstacles determines how far the benefits of expanding treatment extend beyond
health and informs the role of complementary interventions addressing those disadvantages.
These questions are especially pressing for opioid use disorder (OUD): more than 800,000
people died from opioid overdoses in the United States between 1999 and 2023 (Centers for
Disease Control and Prevention, 2025).
We quantify the health and economic returns to expanding access to buprenorphine, a
medication shown in clinical trials to improve treatment retention and reduce illicit opioid
use under controlled conditions (Mattick et al., 2014). We study its delivery in routine
care in the Veterans Health Administration, the largest integrated health system in the
United States. The setting is well-suited to the question. Eligibility for care is stable and
untied to employment, so patients can be followed with essentially no attrition. Because the
Veterans Health Administration (VA) administers social programs alongside care, we observe
health and economic life in the same administrative universe: every clinical encounter and
prescription, complete mortality, enrollment in vocational and disability programs, and, for a
subsample linked to consumer credit records, standing in the credit market. The data cover
more than 140,000 patients with OUD over two decades.
We exploit two sources of quasi-experimental variation in access to buprenorphine treat-
ment. The first is the staggered growth across facilities in the share of clinicians who prescribe
buprenorphine, which until 2023 required a federal “X-waiver” that clinicians obtained and
began using at very different times. We anchor this design on patients’ first opioid overdose
treated in a VA emergency department (ED), an objective marker of severe OUD and a
moment at which treatment is often first offered. In a difference-in-differences design with
1
patient-level panel data, we compare each patient’s change in outcomes with that of patients
who overdosed at the same facility earlier or later in its prescribing expansion, and at other
facilities at the same time, which identifies the policy effect of expanding treatment capacity.
The second is a judge leniency design applied to physicians: within a facility and quarter,
patients with OUD arriving at an ED are assigned essentially at random to physicians who
differ widely and persistently in their propensity to initiate buprenorphine, and we use this
propensity as an instrument for treatment receipt. The first design answers the policymaker’s
question, what expanding treatment capacity buys; the second answers the clinician’s, what
starting treatment does for the patient in front of them.
Wefind that expandingaccess tobuprenorphineimprovespatients’ economiccircumstances
as well as their health. The first step is treatment itself. We measure facility adoption as
the caseload-weighted share of clinicians with prior buprenorphine prescribing experience.
A five percentage point (pp) increase—roughly the gap between facilities at the 10th and
90th percentiles in 2018—raises patients’ buprenorphine use by 10 pp in the month after
an overdose. Averaged over the following two years, the increase in monthly use is 4.7 pp,
roughly doubling the pre-overdose rate. Monthly engagement with substance use disorder
treatment rises 26%.
The economic gains appear in both employment program participation and consumer
credit records. The same expansion in facility prescribing raises enrollment in VA vocational
rehabilitation and employment programs by 1.3 pp, a 65% increase from a 2% baseline.
The judge leniency design extends the evidence to patients’ financial lives. Among nearly
30,000 patients linked to consumer credit records, where the average score of 591 is subprime,
assignment to an ED physician with a 5 pp higher propensity to initiate buprenorphine
raises credit scores by about 5.5 points and increases the probability of crossing into “good”
standing (a score above 670) by 4 pp from a 17% baseline. The improvement is concentrated
in fewer delinquencies and collections, and patients also gain available credit. For scale,
the 5.5 point reduced form effect is of the same order as the 2.4-point gain from a 7 pp
increase in insurance coverage under the Massachusetts reform (Mazumder and Miller, 2016).
Instrumenting buprenorphine receipt with physician propensity yields an estimated 135-point
increase in credit scores (95% confidence interval roughly 18 to 253), a large effect for the
high-risk patients physician assignment moves into treatment. Because veterans receive
nearly free care, relief from medical bills is an unlikely channel; the gains point to a broader
restoration of routine financial functioning.
2
These economic improvements accompany substantial estimated survival gains. The same
five-point increase in clinician adoption reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 3.7 pp,
a 23% reduction in a population where nearly one in six overdose survivors otherwise dies
within two years. An imprecise cause-of-death decomposition suggests reductions in both
drug-related and other deaths, with the latter accounting for most of the estimated decline,
and other health measures move the same way: depression (PHQ-9) scores fall 11%, with no
detectable increase in emergency visits or repeat overdoses. The physician-assignment design
provides additional evidence: assignment to a higher-propensity physician within the same
facility and quarter reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 0.6 pp from a 9% baseline
and raises engagement with care. Instrumenting receipt with physician propensity yields a
13 pp reduction for patients whose treatment physician assignment shifts. That estimate
applies to a high-risk group: these marginal patients would face two-year mortality of roughly
17% without buprenorphine. Both mortality estimates are imprecise, significant at the 10%
level, but stable across specifications. The two designs rest on different assumptions, so their
agreement does not depend on any single one.
Beyond these main results, we ask when the gains arise, for whom, and at what cost.
Treatment uptake and engagement with care respond within a month of the overdose, while
the survival and employment program responses accumulate over the following two years.
This sequence is consistent with treatment engagement preceding economic re-engagement.
Across patients, subgroup estimates suggest the largest survival gains for those in poor
physical health and the largest increases in engagement with care for those with serious
mental illness, suggesting that medication is most life-saving where physical risk is highest
and most valuable as a gateway to care where psychiatric illness is present. Buprenorphine
use rises with little net displacement of methadone, the other main medication for OUD, so
the expansion adds to medication treatment rather than reshuffling it. Finally, at a value
of $300,000 per statistical life-year, our point estimates imply that survival benefits alone
exceed the added medical spending over three years in the VA.
This paper contributes to the literature on the economic value of medical innovation.
Foundational work quantifies the welfare gains from improvements in health and longevity
(Murphy and Topel, 2006; Cutler and McClellan, 2001), while studies of specific technologies
document benefits beyond clinical outcomes, including labor market effects of pain medication,
antidepressant advertising, and radiotherapy (Garthwaite, 2012; Shapiro, 2022; Daysal et al.,
2025). Research on technology diffusion links the adoption of effective treatments to improve-
3
ments in patient survival and healthcare productivity (Skinner and Staiger, 2015). Related
work documents the financial costs of health shocks (Dobkin et al., 2018) and the protection
provided by health insurance (Hu et al., 2018; Mazumder and Miller, 2016; Miller et al., 2021).
We show that medical treatment can contribute to economic recovery from addiction: greater
access to buprenorphine improves financial health as well as survival. We separately identify
the effects of expanding prescribing capacity and of receiving buprenorphine, assessing both
the returns to wider adoption of a medical innovation in routine care and the benefits to
patients who receive the medication.
We also contribute to the literature on substance use disorder (SUD) treatment by
identifying the effects of medication on economic recovery and survival.1 Studies of treatment-
facility openings and closings document effects on drug-related mortality, emergency visits,
and crime (Swensen, 2015; Bullinger, Wang and Feder, 2022; Corredor-Waldron and Currie,
2022; Bondurant, Lindo and Swensen, 2018). The closest studies of expanded access to
buprenorphine find that greater prescriber availability shifts patients toward medication-
based treatment (Barrette, Dafny and Shen, 2023) and that expanded prescribing authority
reduces population opioid mortality (Gui, 2025). We extend this evidence in two ways.
On economic outcomes, we show that treatment improves patients’ financial health and
participation in employment programs.2 On mortality, we identify the effect of receiving
buprenorphine on patients’ all-cause mortality, rather than the population effect of expanded
access.3 We exploit quasi-random assignment to emergency physicians within the same facility
and quarter, accounting for shared changes in facility care that could confound estimates
based on facility adoption.
The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 provides background on
buprenorphine and its regulatory context. Section 3 describes the data, sample, and outcomes
we use. Section 4 outlines our two complementary empirical strategies. Section 5 presents
the main results and robustness checks. Section 6 examines dynamics, heterogeneity, and
mechanisms; Section 7 turns to a cost-benefit calculation and aggregate counterfactuals.
1The broader economics literature on the opioid crisis (reviewed by Maclean et al., 2022) examines the
epidemic’s origins (e.g., Alpert et al., 2022; Schnell, 2026; Finkelstein, Gentzkow and Li, 2025; Eichmeyer and
Zhang, 2022, 2023; Janssen and Zhang, 2023), evaluates supply-side interventions (e.g., Evans, Lieber and
Power, 2019; Buchmueller and Carey, 2018; Soliman, 2025), and documents its economic and intergenerational
costs (Laird and Nielsen, 2016; Currie, Jin and Schnell, 2019; Buckles, Evans and Lieber, 2023).
2Evidence on patients’ economic outcomes includes education and employment following residential SUD
treatment for adolescents (Kim, 2023) and employment following changes in waiting times for outpatient
cannabis treatment (Williams, Bretteville-Jensen and Rose, 2026).
3Also related is work that examines the mortality effects of delays in mental health care among VA
patients (Costantini, 2025).
4
Finally, Section 8 concludes.
2 Background: Buprenorphine
Buprenorphine is a semi-synthetic opioid first approved by the U.S. FDA in 2002 for the
maintenance treatment of opioid use disorder. A single daily dose suppresses withdrawal
and blocks the reinforcing effects of subsequent opioid use (Volkow and Blanco, 2020), and
these properties place it at the center of the World Health Organization’s and the Substance
Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s (SAMHSA) treatment guidelines (World
Health Organization, 2009; Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration,
2021). Unlike methadone, the other widely used medication for OUD, buprenorphine can be
prescribed in office-based settings and dispensed in take-home supplies, sparing most patients
the supervised dosing required at federally regulated opioid treatment programs and allowing
treatment to scale far beyond specialized clinic capacity (Volkow and Blanco, 2020; Blanco
and Volkow, 2019).4 Yet most U.S. patients with OUD receive no treatment at all, and only
about a third of those who do receive medication (Williams et al., 2018).
Prescribing and administering buprenorphine. For most of our study period, prescribing
buprenorphine for OUD outside certified opioid treatment programs required a federal “X-
waiver,” which entailed eight hours of training for physicians (24 for nurse practitioners and
physician assistants) and capped the number of patients a clinician could treat (SAMHSA,
2021). Adoption was slow and highly uneven: beyond the training cost, many clinicians
were reluctant to treat addiction at all, citing stigma, lack of institutional support, and
unfamiliarity with the medication (Blanco and Volkow, 2019). Within the VA, the share of
clinicians who had begun prescribing buprenorphine rose at different times across facilities
over two decades. This staggered, facility-level variation is the basis of our first research
design.5
4Randomized trials establish buprenorphine’s efficacy for treatment retention and reduced illicit opioid
use, but evidence on mortality rests on few trials and very few deaths (Mattick et al., 2014). Observational
studies associate buprenorphine with better health outcomes (e.g., Weiner et al., 2024; Larochelle et al., 2018).
Evidence from other delivery settings links buprenorphine provided during incarceration to lower post-release
recidivism (Evans, Wilson and Friedmann, 2022) and ambulance-based initiation after an overdose to greater
short-term treatment engagement (Carroll et al., 2023).
5The training requirement was relaxed in April 2021 for eligible clinicians treating up to 30 patients,
and the waiver was eliminated in January 2023; studies of both changes find little effect on buprenorphine
treatment (Christine et al., 2024; Chua et al., 2024). These findings are not at odds with our study: we
capture the effect of clinicians’ actual adoption of prescribing, whereas removing a regulatory barrier may
leave other obstacles to adoption in place.
5
Alongside the waiver regime, federal regulation provided a narrower pathway for un-
waivered clinicians, known as the “3-day rule”: any DEA-registered practitioner could
administer (but not prescribe) one day’s dose of buprenorphine to a patient in acute with-
drawal, repeated for up to 72 hours, to stabilize the patient while arranging referral to
formal treatment (U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, 2020). The rule matters most
in emergency departments, where patients in withdrawal frequently present. Whether a
given ED physician uses this authority, however, is largely a matter of individual practice
style: initiation rates vary widely and persistently across physicians working in the same
department.
These two rules generate the variation behind our two empirical strategies. In the facility
adoption difference-in-differences design, the treatment variable is the share of a facility’s
non-ED clinicians who have prescribed or administered buprenorphine, the clinicians able to
provide sustained outpatient treatment; we exclude ED providers, whose 3-day-rule authority
requires no waiver and does not reflect longer term prescribing capacity. The ED physician
propensity design exploits persistent differences across ED physicians in their tendency to
initiate buprenorphine, which the emergency exception makes possible: because any ED
physician can administer it to a patient in withdrawal without a waiver, initiation is a matter
of individual practice style, and the effectively random assignment of unplanned ED arrivals
to physicians on shift turns that variation into quasi-experimental variation in receipt of the
medication at the emergency visit.
3 Data
We analyze data from 2003 through 2025 from the Veterans Health Administration (VA), the
largest integrated healthcare system in the United States, which provides care to more than
9 million eligible veterans through 170 medical centers and over 1,300 outpatient facilities.6
Because eligibility is stable and untied to employment, we observe complete (within-VA)
clinical and program histories, with virtually no insurance-related attrition, among the more
than 140,000 veterans with OUD we study.
Our data cover every healthcare encounter delivered within the VA system (outpatient vis-
its, inpatient admissions, and pharmacy dispensing) with structured diagnosis and procedure
codes, provider and facility identifiers, and time-stamped clinical events. We additionally
6Eligibility includes prior active-duty service, discharge under conditions other than dishonorable, and
either income-based qualification or a service-connected disability.
6
observe rich clinical metrics that are rarely available in claims data, such as structured mental
health assessments (e.g., PHQ-9 depression scores). Beyond medical care, the data link to
VA-administered social programs, including vocational rehabilitation, employment assistance,
and disability compensation, allowing us to track economic and psychosocial outcomes within
the same administrative universe.
To capture care veterans receive outside the VA system, we also link to Medicare Parts A,
B, and D claims (2014–2019), Medicaid claims (2014–2015), and VA-reimbursed community
care records. The latter includes all emergency services delivered at non-VA facilities, which is
particularly important for opioid-related health crises. Finally, we observe complete mortality
data from the CDC National Death Index Plus, including date and cause of death, ensuring
that long-run health outcomes are measured without loss to follow-up.
To measure patients’ financial health, we additionally link veterans to consumer credit
records from TransUnion, one of the three major U.S. credit bureaus. The linkage is built
from a random sample of just over 300,000 veterans with an emergency department visit
between 2014 and 2018, which we provided to TransUnion for matching based on veterans’
social security numbers; approximately 93% of these veterans have at least one credit report
record. For each such veteran, we observe a quarterly panel of credit report information
for the two years before and the two years after the ED visit, including individual-level
data on credit scores and on the balances, credit limits, delinquencies, and third-party
collections reported across open accounts. These records provide a market-based, objectively
reported summary of financial stability that complements the VA’s administrative measures
of economic engagement.
3.1 Sample
In our primary empirical research design, which exploits facility and time variation in provider
buprenorphine adoption rates, we include all VA patients who experience a VA ED visit for an
opioid overdose in the years 2004–2022. We restrict the sample to the patient’s first qualifying
ED opioid overdose event. The rationale for selecting overdose events is twofold. First,
overdoses serve as a highly objective indicator of severe opioid use disorder, increasing the
likelihood these individuals are clinically appropriate candidates for initiating buprenorphine
treatment. Second, by relying on overdose rather than a previous diagnosis of OUD, we avoid
endogenous selection biases related to variation across facilities and time in OUD diagnosis
practices. One might worry that facility-time variation in buprenorphine adoption could itself
7
influence which patients present with an overdose; we find no evidence of such compositional
selection (Section 5.3).
Our second strategy uses all VA patients with an ED visit between 2004 and 2022
and an OUD diagnosis in the prior year, again keeping each patient’s first qualifying visit.
Conditioning on a prior diagnosis rather than an overdose is possible here because the design
compares patients assigned to different physicians within a facility and quarter, so facility-level
variation in diagnosis practice cannot confound it, and it yields a sample nearly twenty times
larger, which the IV analysis needs.
Our analysis of financial outcomes applies this second strategy to the TransUnion-linked
subsample: veterans with an ED visit between 2014 and 2018, again keeping each patient’s
first qualifying visit and requiring a prior-year OUD diagnosis. Among the 82,889 patients
meeting these criteria, 35.7% have an observed credit score and enter the financial outcomes
sample.7
In all samples, we drop terminal cancer and end-of-life geriatric patients, as well as
patients who die within seven days of the ED encount

[…]

sponse diminishes thereafter:
the estimated increase averages 5.6 pp in months 1–6, 3.1 pp in months 7–12, 2 pp in months
13–18, and 1.6 pp in months 19–24 (Table 2). A sizable response thus remains in the final six
months: the point estimate retains approximately 16% of the initial increase, although it
is imprecise. This decline need not reflect waning engagement alone. Because facility-level
adoption is measured at the index quarter, exposure differences narrow over the window as
lower-adoption facilities catch up, and the composition of surviving patients shifts.16
The survival and employment-program responses develop more gradually than the initial
increase in treatment use. By month 6, the estimated reduction in cumulative mortality
16Monthly non-mortality outcomes are measured among surviving patients. Appendix C reports bounds
assessing sensitivity to changes in survivor composition.
24
is approximately 43% of its month-24 value, while the increase in monthly vocational
rehabilitation participation is approximately 70% of its month-24 value (Figure 5).
Two conclusions follow. First, the response to the crisis moment is not transient. Medica-
tion use and engagement with care remain elevated two years after the overdose, though at
a fraction of their initial level. Thus, the adherence concern raised in the introduction is a
matter of degree: engagement attenuates but does not disappear. Second, the sequence is
consistent with treatment engagement facilitating economic re-engagement, with treatment
responding first and survival and employment-program gains following over the subsequent
two years.
The timing also matters for valuation. The costs of expanded adoption arrive mostly
in the first year while the survival benefits build over time, which is why the cost-benefit
calculation in Section 7.1 turns positive only in the third year.
6.2 Heterogeneity
Medications for OUD may not translate into broad and sustained life improvements for
everyone. Even if adherence is achieved, health gains may not automatically spill over into
economic or psychosocial domains, especially for patients burdened by severe co-morbidities
or serious mental illness. To probe these possibilities, we examine whether the effects of
buprenorphine access differ systematically across patient subgroups defined by their prior
health status and treatment history.
We consider four natural margins of heterogeneity, each intended to capture a distinct
dimension of baseline patient risk. First, we split patients by whether their number of prior
Elixhauser comorbidities is above or below the median, using this as a summary measure of
their overall physical health. Second, we separate patients by the presence or absence of a
serious mental illness diagnosis (such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or major depressive
disorder) in the prior year, to test whether psychiatric conditions influence patients’ ability
to benefit. Third, we distinguish between patients who did or did not receive buprenorphine
treatment in the year prior to their overdose, using this as a proxy for OUD severity and
prior engagement with treatment. Fourth, we split patients by whether they are of working
age. For each subgroup, we re-estimate our facility-level adoption design, and present the
results in Figure 6.
For medically sick patients, the return to medication appears to be survival rather than
economic re-engagement. Patients with above-median Elixhauser scores have larger estimated
25
survival gains from buprenorphine access but smaller estimated increases in vocational
rehabilitation participation than healthier patients, though the difference in mortality effects
is imprecisely estimated (interaction p-value 0.11). The smaller economic response is likely
a matter of age: patients with more comorbidities are also older, and for many of them
returning to work is no longer realistic, which is what the age split below shows.
For patients with serious mental illness, medication appears to work mainly as a gateway
to care. Their estimated increases in engagement with medical care are the largest of any
group: outpatient visits and both mental and physical health encounters rise more sharply
once buprenorphine is available. Their estimated survival improvement is smaller than for
patients without serious mental illness, plausibly because a larger share of their baseline
mortality risk runs through causes, such as suicide and chronic disease, that medication for
OUD addresses only indirectly.
Prior buprenorphine users, patients who had already initiated treatment at some point
before their overdose, respond strongly across every margin. They show higher gains in
outpatient engagement, more pronounced survival benefits, and a larger boost in vocational
rehabilitation enrollment, despite a smaller increase in buprenorphine uptake itself (since
many were already on the medication). Because prior users are, by construction, patients
already engaged with treatment, this pattern admits two readings: larger treatment effects for
patients already connected to care, or favorable selection into prior use; we do not distinguish
them here. This group’s uptake response is smallest while its outcome responses are largest,
suggesting a large effect per unit of induced treatment.
Finally, the age split sharpens the interpretation of the economic effects and helps
disentangle the comorbidity results above, since worse physical health and older age are
strongly correlated in our sample. The vocational rehabilitation response is concentrated
largely among patients of prime working age (we split at 55, the upper bound of the standard
25–54 prime working age definition), at 1.8 pp versus 0.7 pp for patients 55 and older (panel (d)
of Figure 6), though the difference between age groups is not statistically distinguishable. The
pattern is consistent with enrollment in employment programs reflecting genuine movement
toward work among those for whom work is a feasible margin, rather than an artifact
of program reclassification. Survival gains, by contrast, are larger among older patients,
indicating that the life-saving and economic margins of buprenorphine operate on partially
distinct subpopulations.
These findings speak to the motivating question of whether and for whom medical
26
innovation translates into real-world improvements. Taken together, the heterogeneity results
show that buprenorphine’s benefits are not evenly distributed. They appear most life-saving
for those in poor physical health, largest for care engagement among those with serious
mental illness, most broad-based for those who had prior exposure to treatment, and, on the
economic margin, operative chiefly among those of working age.
6.3 Substitution from Methadone
Buprenorphine and methadone are the two most widely used evidence-based, first-line
treatments for opioid use disorder. It is therefore natural to ask whether expanding access
to one therapy simply displaces patients from the other; answering this question clarifies
whether the benefits we estimate reflect a reallocation of existing patients across medications
or extensive margin responses of engaging new patients in MOUD treatment. To do so,
we re-estimate our baseline facility adoption empirical design for the outcome of a patient
receiving methadone treatment in a given month.
The estimated effect on methadone use is 0.6 pp and statistically indistinguishable from
zero (Table A.9). The 95% confidence interval excludes a net decline larger than approximately
0.4 pp, less than a tenth of the 4.7 pp increase in buprenorphine use. Thus, substitution from
methadone can account for at most a small share of the gain in buprenorphine treatment.
Similarly, assignment to an ED physician with a higher buprenorphine prescribing propensity
has no detectable effect on emergency methadone treatment or referral to an opioid treatment
program at the index visit (Table C.1). The improvements we document therefore come
largely from drawing new patients onto evidence-based medication rather than reshuffling
existing patients across therapies.
7 Policy Implications
7.1 Cost-Benefit Analysis
We conduct a cost-benefit calculation that compares the value of the estimated survival
gains with the medical and medication costs of expanding buprenorphine prescribing. We
consider the same five-point increase in the caseload-weighted share of clinicians with prior
buprenorphine prescribing experience, approximately the gap between facilities at the 10th
and 90th percentiles in 2018. We measure the gains in life-years, the extra time that patients
live within each period, and put a dollar value on each life-year. We use $300,000 per
27
statistical life-year as our central benchmark, informed by the life-year valuations in Murphy
and Topel (2006).17 This asks whether survival alone can justify the extra spending, before
placing any value on improvements in patients’ wellbeing or economic circumstances. All
amounts are averages over all overdose patients in the sample. They add up costs or benefits
over the first one, two, or three years after the overdose.
For a 5 pp increase in facility prescribing adoption, the estimated additional cost over three
years is $8,087 per overdose patient: $7,572 in medical spending and $515 in buprenorphine.
The estimated survival gain is 0.0347 life-years per patient, worth approximately $10,400 at
the $300,000 valuation. The resulting net benefit is approximately $2,300 per patient.18 The
balance is less favorable over shorter horizons: most added costs arise in the first year, while
survival benefits accumulate over time, leaving net benefits negative after one and two years.
Table 6 reports the results for each time horizon.
The conclusion depends on the value assigned to an additional year of life. Over three
years, benefits and costs break even at approximately $233,000 per life-year. At $200,000,
costs exceed benefits by $1,148 per patient; at $400,000, benefits exceed costs by $5,792.
Discounting future costs and benefits at 3% annually reduces the net benefit at the $300,000
valuation to approximately $1,900.
For perspective, our estimated cost of $233,000 per life-year gained is similar in magnitude
to the approximately $220,000 in direct budgetary costs per life-year gained from Medicaid
expansions estimated by Wyse and Meyer (2025), expressed in 2024 dollars.19 Their calculation
includes projected gains over patients’ remaining lifetimes, while ours counts only life-years
gained within three years of the overdose. The comparison therefore provides a benchmark
for scale rather than a ranking of the interventions.
The positive balance is subject to uncertainty in the estimated survival gains and spending;
we do not report a confidence interval for net benefits. For simplicity and clarity, the
calculation also omits some costs and benefits. Costs exclude the expense of increasing
adoption itself, such as clinician training. At the central valuation, our point estimates
leave approximately $2,300 per overdose patient to cover such implementation costs within
the three-year calculation. Benefits exclude survival gains beyond the three-year horizon.
17Murphy and Topel (2006) use a baseline value of $373,000 for a life-year for a 50-year-old man, expressed
in 2004 dollars. Our $300,000 benchmark is expressed in 2024 dollars, and we examine sensitivity to lower
and higher valuations below.
18Appendix D describes the construction of these figures.
19Their reported estimate is $179,000 in 2019 dollars; we convert it to 2024 dollars using the annual-average
CPI-U.
28
Improvements in depression and participation in vocational rehabilitation and employment
programs also remain unvalued.
7.2 Aggregate Counterfactuals
We use the above mentioned cost and benefit estimates to illustrate what wider buprenorphine
adoption could mean for patients who have overdosed.20 We first consider one future year of
overdose patients in the VA, taking a cohort of 500 patients.21 If the estimated per-patient
effects and costs apply to this cohort, a 5 pp increase in facility prescribing adoption would
imply approximately 19 fewer deaths over the following two years and $1.2 million in net
benefits over three years, valuing each additional life-year at $300,000 (Table D.1).
We also ask what the same expansion could have achieved for the overdose patients
treated over our study period. Across the 7,517 patients in our facility-adoption sample, a
5 pp increase in prescribing adoption implies approximately 278 fewer deaths within two
years and 261 life-years gained over three years. At $300,000 per life-year, the three-year
survival benefits amount to $78.2 million, compared with $60.8 million in added medical and
buprenorphine costs.
These calculations illustrate the stakes of wider adoption: under our central assumptions,
bringing an existing medication to more patients could yield substantial survival gains whose
value exceeds the additional medical spending.
8 Conclusion
Medical treatment can contribute to economic recovery from addiction. Our evidence from
the Veterans Health Administration shows that expanding access to buprenorphine produces
benefits in routine care. A 5 pp increase in prescribing adoption raises treatment uptake and
engagement with care and reduces two-year mortality by an estimated 23% in a population
where one in six patients otherwise dies. The benefits extend beyond health: participation
in employment programs rises, and the physician-assignment design provides evidence of
improvedfinancialhealth. Thesefindingsshowthatthedisadvantagesaccompanyingaddiction
need not prevent economic gains from treatment. At a value of $300,000 per statistical
life-year, our point estimates imply that survival benefits alone exceed the added medical
spending over three years.
20All calculations use the facility-adoption-based causal effect point estimates and inherit the uncertainty
in the estimated survival gains and spending effects.
21During 2020–2024, approximately 490 VA patients per year presented to an ED with an opioid overdose.
29
The benefits develop over time. Treatment use and engagement with care rise promptly,
while gains in survival and employment-program participation emerge more gradually. This
pattern is consistent with treatment engagement supporting economic recovery. Whether
complementary social and employment supports can strengthen that recovery remains an
important question. Our findings also highlight the role of adoption in realizing the value of
medical innovation. Studies of relaxed training requirements and X-waiver elimination find
limited growth in the number of patients receiving treatment (Christine et al., 2024; Chua
et al., 2024); our estimates show the potential gains when expanded prescribing capacity
brings patients into care. Policies that help clinicians incorporate buprenorphine into routine
practice, through training, institutional support, and reimbursement, may therefore be
important complements to regulatory reform.
Several caveats apply. The estimates come from an older, predominantly male veteran
population treated in an integrated health system; our economic measures include credit
records and program participation, but not observed employment or earnings; and the
physician-design estimates apply to patients whose treatment physician assignment shifts,
who are at higher risk than the average patient with OUD. The estimates also capture
only effects on the patient. Treatment may generate additional benefits for spouses and
intergenerational impacts through children and other family members. Finally, the size of
the estimated gains makes clinician adoption itself an important object of study: identifying
which barriers matter most, and which policies actually increase prescribing, is the next step
in converting clinical efficacy into recovery from one of the deadliest public health crises in
U.S. history.
30

One of the key parts of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) decision finding Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya was the inclusion of sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) in the Court’s reasoning.
The ICJ’s Gambia v Myanmar decision represents a much more comprehensive understanding of what genocide encompasses than in some (or even much) of the past jurisprudence, including its own. In the cases brought against Serbia in the ICJ, the Court only found that what occurred in Srebrenica constituted genocide, in keeping with the findings of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. Gambia v Myanmar goes beyond the focus on genocide as killing, engaging substantially with other genocidal crimes – including SGBV.
The judgment addressed two types of sexual and gender-based violence, particularly against women, that were part of this case: rape (and sexual violence), and imposition of measures intended to prevent births. These crimes were comprehensively recognised by the ICJ as an integral part of the genocide against the Rohingya, as specific crimes and as evidence of genocidal intent.
A Dearth of Attention to Sexual and Gender-Based Violence in Genocide Before International Courts
There has generally been insufficient attention paid by international courts and tribunals to sexual and gender-based violence against women in the context of international crimes, but particularly so for the crime of genocide. Over the years, there have been advances, but gaps remain, despite feminist scholars and practitioners framing sexual and gender-based violence as part of the genocide process, including the Rohingya genocide.
It was only at the push of feminist advocates and then-judge Navi Pillay (incidentally, an ad hoc judge on the bench for Gambia v Myanmar) that rape featured as part of the Akayesu case in the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR).
However, few other ICTR cases resulted in convictions for sexual violence, and that Tribunal’s subsequent treatment of sexual violence has been criticised. In the ICTY, there was no finding of genocide other than the gendered killing of boys and men at Srebrenica, despite the extensive and systematic sexual and gender-based violence against Bosnian girls and women, including rape camps. Such violence was recognised in convictions for war crimes and crimes against humanity. Thus, while the case law contributed to the development of the definition of rape and other forms of sexual violence, there was no engagement with the idea of sexual violence as genocide even though such sexual violence has had long-term impacts on Bosnian women.
Rape and Sexual Violence
Rape, including gang rape, was a ubiquitous part of the violence against the Rohingya, directed predominantly against girls and women. The Court would have been remiss if rape had not formed a significant part of its ruling, and the Court blatantly found “extensive acts of rape and other forms of violence” were committed by Myanmar’s security forces, with rape and gang rape “a notable and recurrent feature of the violence” (para. 254).
At no point was the definition of rape discussed; the Court simply took its reference to rape as a given, which demonstrates the acceptance of this crime in the context of international crimes. The Court also determined that the exact number of victims is difficult to establish due to stigma, but noted at least 1,834 victims were listed in one report (paras. 258, 335). However, the Court held that “it need not set out the precise extent of the injuries suffered or make a conclusive finding on the number of victims” to find that serious physical or mental harm occurred. This is an appropriate finding, given that it is impossible to have an exact number of victims of sexual violence, and it is generally assumed that the number of victims is always higher than any figure that may be produced.
Rapes were committed with particular brutality, usually in public, often gang rapes, in front of family members, and frequently including mutilation. The “extreme physical brutality” of the rapes was acknowledged, as was the rape of pregnant women, and the fact that such violence was also committed with mutilation of the victims (including breasts and genitalia) (paras. 255-6). There are also reports of sexual violence against boys and men (mentioned in paras. 254, 260, 369).
The Court also included sexual violence as a component of its discussion on attacks on children. Here, the judges specifically positioned children as victims of sexual violence. The judgment draws attention to several individual cases, with girls as young as 9 raped (para. 260).
The decision considered rape within the context of Article II(b) causing serious bodily or mental harm, acts under which must be intentional. The Court drew from several intervening states’ submissions that “the harm resulting from sexual and gender-based violence is ‘almost universally’ » serious « by its nature” (para. 324). It confirmed its previous finding in the Serbia cases that rape and SGBV can constitute the actus reus of genocide under Article II(b). It confirmed that the widespread rape and sexual violence committed by Myanmar’s security forces “resulted in serious physical harm” (para. 329).
The Court also took into account the trauma caused by the “brutal sexual violence”, which has resulted in long-term physical, as well as psychological, social and community effects (para. 257). It categorised the rape and sexual violence as contributing “to lasting mental harm to survivors, as well as to those who witnessed the acts” (para. 331). The Court found these acts intentional and committed with knowledge that they would cause serious mental harm (para. 334), and was “fully convinced” that the violence of 2017 “caused serious bodily and mental harm to a very significant number of” Rohingya.
The SGBV was deemed to be genocidal, because “sexual violence not only physically and mentally harms the victims, it can also be a step in the process of degrading and destroying a human group by causing the ‘destruction of the spirit, of the will to live, and of life itself’” (para. 417, citing Akayesu para. 732). In taking into account the physical and mental harm of the sexual violence, the widespread nature of the rapes, and the extreme brutality of the rapes, the Court held that “Myanmar’s security forces committed sexual violence against members of the Rohingya population in a way that degraded the victims and their communities to an extreme degree” (para. 420). The sexual violence was framed as an act that violates “the foundations of the Rohingya group” (para. 416).
Imposition of Measures Intended to Prevent Births
The majority judgment deemed measures intended to prevent births (Article II(d)) (which can also be termed reproductive violence) to encompass “measures intended to bring about the failure of the group ‘to live and reproduce normally’” (para. 360, citing the ICTY). Importantly, the judgment confirmed that such measures do not have to be successful, just intended to prevent births (para. 362). This is a welcome departure from the Court’s ruling in Croatia v Serbia, an erroneous application of the provision, which is clearly worded “measures intended to prevent births”, not “measures that prevent births”. In Croatia v Serbia (para. 166, emphasis added), the Court stated that rape could only be considered to fall under Article II(d) if “the circumstances of the commission of [acts of sexual violence], and their consequences, are such that the capacity of members of the group to procreate is affected”.
In the current case, the Court held that both the physical and psychological impact of birth prevention measures are relevant, including the social and cultural context, for example where victims of sexual violence are stigmatised (para. 361). In applying this broad view, the Court considered two main types of conduct committed by Myanmar’s security forces and the government to be measures intended to prevent births.
Unsurprisingly, rape was a key part of this crime. The Court held that “the magnitude and character of the acts of sexual violence… support the conclusion that the acts were intended to physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the population to procreate” (para. 366). The Court again drew attention to the brutality of the rapes, including gang rapes, mass rapes, rape of pregnant women, extreme violence against girls and young women, rape of girls, and the additional physical violence accompanying the rapes, such as mutilation. The long-term physical and mental consequences of the rapes was noted, including “physical harm to reproductive functioning”, as well as trauma, social ostracisation and cultural stigma (paras. 367-8).
Beyond that, the Court also included a range of discriminatory measures that Myanmar had imposed on the Rohingya over the decades, including through legislative means, as measures intended to prevent births (paras. 363-5, 401). These measures were restrictions on Muslim marriages, restrictions on birth (expressly stated to be a measure against the Rohingya and only imposed against the Rohingya), and “denial of birth registration and issuance of birth certificates for Rohingya children” (para. 365). Such measures were considered part of a broader context of culpable acts that were “systematically directed against the Rohingya” (para. 399).
These two categories of acts were found to “establish an intent to impact the capacity of members of the Rohingya community to reproduce normally and thus an intent to prevent births within the group”, convincing the Court of the commission of the actus reus of Article II(d) (paras. 370-1).
A Strong Judgment
The prominence of SGBV in The Gambia v. Myanmar decision cannot be overstated. That forms of SGBV were positioned in the ruling as such a key part of the genocide process against the Rohingya not only demonstrates that the Court has developed a more sophisticated understanding of genocide and genocidal intent, but also that it is recognising the gendered nature of the crime overall.
In one sense, the Court is simply applying the law, because it is clear and well acknowledged that rape causes serious bodily and mental harm. However, the Court’s recognition of a system of human rights restrictions that had long-lasting social and cultural impact on the Rohingya people’s ability to procreate as the crime of measures intended to prevent births, adds something new to the jurisprudence.
This judgment captures the reality of what happened to the Rohingya, and more broadly, what the genocide process actually entails. It is reflective of what genocide scholars have long been writing about: that genocide is more than killing, it is gendered, and long-term discriminatory and persecutory policies that do not necessarily involve physical violence are an integral part of the process.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said earlier this week that the European Union's proposed 22nd sanctions package against Russia would ban tankers insured in Russia and add more than 70 vessels to the bloc's list of designated “shadow fleet” ships.
The package would also prohibit European companies from helping construct, operate or repair Russian energy facilities, refineries included, and would apply energy services restrictions to electricity services for the first time.
The package requires the approval of all 27 EU member states.
"The aim is to keep pressure on Russia to end their war of aggression in Ukraine,” von der Leyen said. “And we will continue to propose new sanctions until Russia shows genuine intent for a lasting peace in Ukraine.”
The announcement did not define "insured in Russia". Possible tests include the direct insurer's domicile, the place where the policy is placed, ownership, or Russian participation in co-insurance or reinsurance.
The announcement also did not say whether the test extends beyond P&I cover, whether transits of the Danish straits would be covered, or when the ban would apply.
According to Platts, an S&P Global analysis found no oil or chemical tankers insured by Russian firms among vessels that had discharged cargo in the Netherlands in November up to the time of its analysis. Lloyd's List reported that Russian or Russia-linked cover was declared for roughly one in three tanker transits in the Baltic.
Among the 166 shadow fleet tankers it tracked carrying Russian oil in August, KSE Institute identified Russian insurance for 52. At least one of the six jurisdictions it monitors had sanctioned 48 of the ships, and 15 flew the Russian flag.
Under existing rules, vessels listed in Annex XLII of Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 are generally barred from EU ports and specified services. If the insurance ban is applied to port calls, it could exclude an unlisted tanker carrying non-Russian cargo on insurance grounds alone.
Maritime claims certificates required under Directive 2009/20/EC already name the insurer and its principal place of business. A genuine certificate confirms that cover exists but does not establish whether the insurer would pass a separate sanctions test.
Norway's financial regulator ordered Norway-registered Romarine to stop unauthorised activities on March 4, 2025, and later publicly warned that the firm was not registered as an insurance provider.
Romarine said it operated in line with applicable regulations.
Germany began asking passing tankers about their oil pollution liability cover in July 2025.
Tanya Stepanova of S&P Global Energy CERA told Platts that European firms had withdrawn from Russia's refining sector almost immediately after the war began.
"For that reason, I do not expect the immediate impact of this sanction package to be material," she said.
The EU's 21st package, adopted in July, added 41 vessels to the designated list.
